title: The Mean (AVERAGE)
learning_objective: Calculate the mean of a dataset in Excel using AVERAGE, and explain what the resulting figure represents for planning purposes.
description_for_ai: The mean (average) is the sum of all values divided by the number of values, calculated in Excel as =AVERAGE(range). It represents a single figure that levels out every value in the dataset as though performance were spread equally across every day, transaction, or record. The mean uses every data point in its calculation, which makes it sensitive to unusually large or small values: one extreme day can pull the mean noticeably higher or lower than where most of the data actually sits. An analyst reports the mean when they want one representative planning figure, such as average daily customers or average daily sales, but the mean on its own does not reveal whether that figure is being distorted by an unusual day.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Including the header row in the AVERAGE range, which Excel either errors on or silently ignores. Reporting the mean as 'the typical day' without checking whether it is being pulled upward or downward by an unusually high or low value. Using 'mean' and 'average' as if they were different statistics, when they are the same thing.
example_code_for_ai:
=AVERAGE(D5:D34)
' Returns 112.87 for a branch's 30 days of daily customer counts
' One unusually high day (a promotion) is included and pulls this figure upward

title: The Median (MEDIAN)
learning_objective: Calculate the median of a dataset in Excel using MEDIAN, and explain it as the middle value when data is sorted from smallest to largest.
description_for_ai: The median is the middle value of a dataset once every value is sorted from smallest to largest, calculated in Excel as =MEDIAN(range). If there is an odd number of values, the median is the single middle one; if there is an even number, the median is the average of the two middle values. Unlike the mean, the median only depends on which value occupies the middle position, so a single extremely high or low value does not shift it much. This makes the median a more honest 'typical value' when a dataset contains an unusual extreme, because half of all values fall below it and half fall above it regardless of how extreme the outliers are.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming the median must always equal one of the actual data points, forgetting that an even-count dataset averages the two middle values. Believing the median and mean will always be close together, and being confused when a dataset shows them far apart. Sorting the data manually and miscounting the middle position on a large dataset instead of trusting the MEDIAN function.
example_code_for_ai:
=MEDIAN(D5:D34)
' Returns 96 for the same 30-day customer dataset where AVERAGE returned 112.87
' The gap between 96 and 112.87 signals an unusual high value is present

title: The Mode (MODE.SNGL)
learning_objective: Calculate the mode of a dataset in Excel using MODE.SNGL, and explain it as the single most frequently occurring value.
description_for_ai: The mode is the value that appears most often in a dataset, calculated in Excel as =MODE.SNGL(range). Unlike the mean and median, the mode is not a calculated centre, it simply reports which exact value recurs the most. A dataset can have one mode, several tied modes, or no mode at all if every value is different. MODE.SNGL specifically returns only the first mode encountered when there is a tie; a different function, MODE.MULT, would be needed to list every tied mode as an array. The mode is most useful when an analyst wants to know the single most common recurring figure, such as the most frequent daily customer count, which is a different question from 'what is typical on average.'
common_mistakes_for_ai: Expecting MODE.SNGL to return an error or a range when there are multiple tied modes, rather than understanding it silently returns just the first one found. Treating the mode as a measure of central tendency equivalent to the mean or median, when it answers a different question entirely. Applying the mode to a dataset where every value is unique and being surprised by the #N/A result rather than recognising that no mode exists.
example_code_for_ai:
=MODE.SNGL(D5:D34)
' Returns 82 for the 30-day customer dataset
' 82 customers was recorded on four separate days, more than any other single value

title: The Range (MAX - MIN)
learning_objective: Calculate the range of a dataset in Excel using MAX and MIN, and explain it as a quick, rough measure of how spread out the data is.
description_for_ai: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest value in a dataset, calculated in Excel as =MAX(range)-MIN(range). It measures the total width of the data from worst to best, using only two values out of the entire dataset. Because it ignores everything except the two extremes, a single unusually high or low value can make the range look far larger than what a typical day actually looks like. The range is a fast first check for volatility before deeper analysis, not a complete picture of spread on its own.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing =MAX(range)-MIN(range) with mismatched or incorrect ranges for MAX versus MIN, producing a meaningless result. Treating a large range as proof that most days are wildly different from each other, rather than recognising it may reflect just one or two extreme days. Assuming the range and the standard deviation measure the same thing, when the range only uses two data points and the standard deviation uses all of them.
example_code_for_ai:
=MAX(D5:D34)-MIN(D5:D34)
' Returns 345 for the 30-day customer dataset (420 maximum minus 75 minimum)
' A single promotion day, not a generally chaotic month, is driving this wide range

title: Standard Deviation (STDEV.S)
learning_objective: Calculate the sample standard deviation of a dataset in Excel using STDEV.S, and interpret it as the typical distance of a value from the mean.
description_for_ai: The sample standard deviation measures, on average, how far each value in a dataset sits from the mean, calculated in Excel as =STDEV.S(range) when the data is a sample rather than a complete population. It is expressed in the same units as the original data, for example customers or naira, not squared units. A small standard deviation means values cluster tightly around the mean and are easy to plan around; a large standard deviation means values swing widely and day-to-day performance is harder to predict. STDEV.S divides by (n-1), the sample-adjustment used when the data represents a sample of possible days rather than every day that could ever occur; the population version, STDEV.P, divides by n instead and should not be used on a sample.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Using STDEV.P instead of STDEV.S on a dataset that is a sample, not the full population, which understates the true spread. Interpreting a large standard deviation as an error in the data rather than as a genuine signal of volatility. Forgetting that standard deviation is in the same units as the original data, and mistakenly comparing it directly to a percentage or a squared value like variance.
example_code_for_ai:
=STDEV.S(D5:D34)
' Returns 61.71 for the 30-day customer dataset
' Excluding the one promotion day drops this to 21.42, showing how much a single value inflated the spread

title: Choosing Mean vs Median for Skewed Data
learning_objective: Given a dataset's calculated mean and median, decide which one to report as the 'typical' figure and justify the choice based on how far apart the two values are.
description_for_ai: A dataset is skewed when a small number of unusually high or low values pull it away from where most of the data actually sits. When a dataset is not skewed, the mean and median sit close together and either is a fair summary. When a dataset is skewed by one or more extreme values, the mean is pulled toward those extremes while the median stays close to where most of the data actually is, because the median only depends on position, not magnitude. The decision rule an analyst applies: if the mean and median are close together, report the mean, because it uses every data point; if they diverge noticeably, report the median, because it better represents a typical case when extreme values are present. This is a judgement call based on comparing the two already-calculated values, not a new formula.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Defaulting to always reporting the mean out of habit, even when it has already been shown to diverge sharply from the median. Treating any small numeric difference between mean and median as automatic proof of skew, rather than judging whether the gap is meaningfully large relative to the data. Reporting the median without first checking whether the underlying cause is a genuine outlier worth explaining separately, rather than just picking the 'safer-looking' number.
example_code_for_ai:
' No new formula: this micro-topic reuses AVERAGE and MEDIAN results already calculated
Mean = 112.87, Median = 96   ' noticeably far apart -> report the median as the typical day
Mean = 110.5, Median = 111.5 ' close together -> either figure is a fair summary, mean is fine

title: Outliers and Their Effect on Summary Statistics
learning_objective: Identify an outlier in a dataset and explain how it distorts the mean, range, and standard deviation compared to the median, without deleting it from the dataset.
description_for_ai: An outlier is a value that sits unusually far from the rest of the dataset, either much higher or much lower. Outliers are not automatically errors: some are genuine events (a promotion, a public holiday, a system outage) and some are mistakes (a typo, a duplicate entry), and part of an analyst's job is telling the two apart before deciding what to do. An outlier pulls the mean strongly toward itself because the mean uses every value; the median barely moves because it only depends on which value sits in the middle position; the range and standard deviation both increase sharply because both measure spread, and an outlier is by definition far from the rest of the data. The professional habit is to calculate summary statistics twice, once including a suspected outlier and once excluding it, compare the two sets of results, and report both the excluding-outlier figure as the 'typical' value and the outlier itself as a separately explained event. An outlier is never quietly deleted from the underlying dataset.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Deleting the outlier row from the dataset instead of excluding it only from the specific calculation being reported. Assuming every outlier must be a data-entry error without first considering a genuine business explanation, such as a promotion or holiday. Reporting only the with-outlier or only the without-outlier statistics, rather than showing both and explaining the difference to the reader.
example_code_for_ai:
' With the outlier included:
=AVERAGE(D5:D34)   -> 112.87
=STDEV.S(D5:D34)   -> 61.71
' With the outlier excluded (two ranges, data left in place, not deleted):
=AVERAGE(D5:D31,D33:D34)   -> 102.28
=STDEV.S(D5:D31,D33:D34)   -> 21.42

title: Building a Scatter Plot to See a Relationship
learning_objective: Build a scatter plot in Excel from two numeric columns, and read whether the resulting shape suggests a positive, negative, or absent relationship before calculating any statistic.
description_for_ai: A scatter plot places one variable on the horizontal axis and a second variable on the vertical axis, plotting one dot per record, built in Excel via Insert > Charts > Scatter after selecting the two numeric columns. Three basic shapes to recognise: a positive relationship shows dots trending upward left to right, a negative relationship shows dots trending downward left to right, and no relationship shows dots scattered with no visible pattern. Building the chart before calculating a correlation coefficient lets an analyst visually confirm the relationship looks like a straight line and spot any outlier points, rather than trusting a single summary number blind.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Selecting the two columns in the wrong order, which swaps which variable lands on which axis and can flip how the trend reads. Skipping the chart entirely and jumping straight to a correlation coefficient, missing an outlier or a curved shape that the number alone would hide. Choosing a Line chart instead of a Scatter chart, which forces the x-axis into equal spacing and misrepresents the true relationship between two numeric variables.
example_code_for_ai:
' Select columns C (Marketing Spend) and D (Daily Sales), then Insert > Charts > Scatter
' Resulting dots trend upward, left to right, with some scatter around the trend
' That upward shape is checked visually before any CORREL formula is calculated

title: The Correlation Coefficient (CORREL)
learning_objective: Calculate the correlation coefficient between two variables in Excel using CORREL, and state that it always falls between -1 and +1.
description_for_ai: The correlation coefficient, written r, measures how strongly and in which direction two variables move together, calculated in Excel as =CORREL(range1,range2) where both ranges contain the same number of paired values. r always falls between -1 and +1: values close to +1 indicate a strong positive relationship, values close to -1 indicate a strong negative relationship, and values close to 0 indicate little to no straight-line relationship. CORREL requires the two ranges to be equal in length and matched row by row, since it treats each pair of values (one from each range, same row) as one observation.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Passing two ranges of different lengths into CORREL, which produces a #N/A error. Selecting ranges that are not row-aligned, for example one range shifted by a row relative to the other, which silently pairs the wrong values together. Reporting r without its sign, losing the information about whether the relationship is positive or negative.
example_code_for_ai:
=CORREL(C5:C28,D5:D28)
' Returns 0.78 for 24 days of marketing spend (C) against daily sales (D) at one branch
' Returns 0.27 for the identical experiment run at a second branch
not_yet_taught: reading the strength and direction of a correlation

title: Reading the Strength and Direction of r
learning_objective: Given a calculated correlation coefficient, classify it using a strength scale and translate it into a plain-language business statement.
description_for_ai: A commonly used rough guide for describing the strength of a correlation coefficient, regardless of sign: 0.0 to 0.2 is very weak or no relationship, 0.2 to 0.4 is weak, 0.4 to 0.7 is moderate, and 0.7 to 1.0 is strong. The sign of r determines direction (positive or negative), and the magnitude determines strength; these bands are a communication convention, not a fixed scientific threshold, and different contexts may use different cutoffs. A correlation coefficient should never be reported to a non-technical audience as a bare number; it should always be paired with a plain-language statement of both its strength and direction, for example describing r = 0.78 as 'a strong positive relationship' rather than leaving the number to speak for itself.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating the strength bands as fixed scientific law rather than a rough communication convention that can vary by context. Reporting only the numeric value of r to a manager without translating it into strength and direction in plain language. Confusing a weak correlation (for example r = 0.27) with an invalid or incorrectly calculated one, when it is simply a genuine, real finding.
example_code_for_ai:
' No new formula: this micro-topic classifies an already-calculated r value
r = 0.78  -> falls in the 0.7-1.0 band -> "a strong positive relationship"
r = 0.27  -> falls in the 0.2-0.4 band -> "a weak positive relationship"

title: Correlation Is Not Causation
learning_objective: Explain, using a concrete example, why a strong correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other.
description_for_ai: A correlation coefficient measures that two variables move together; it does not identify why they move together. Two correlated variables can be related for at least three different reasons: one variable genuinely causes the other, a third hidden factor (a confounding variable) causes both, or the relationship is coincidental, especially likely in a small dataset. The standard illustrative example: ice cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in the same weeks each year, but ice cream does not cause sunburn, hot sunny weather drives both. The professional standard is to treat a strong correlation as a reason to investigate further, never as grounds to announce a cause, and to always ask what a believable direct mechanism between the two variables would actually be before making a causal claim.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Stating that a strong correlation 'proves' or 'shows conclusively' that one variable causes another. Assuming causation must run in a specific direction (X causes Y) without considering that Y could cause X, or that both could be driven by a third factor. Treating a low correlation as evidence against causation entirely, when a real causal relationship can still produce a weak linear correlation if the true relationship is not a straight line.
example_code_for_ai:
' Conceptual, no formula: ice cream sales and sunburn cases correlate strongly in summer
' Correlation coefficient between them would be high, but neither variable causes the other
' A third factor, hot sunny weather, drives both figures upward at the same time

title: Spotting a Spurious Relationship (Confounding Variables)
learning_objective: Given a strong correlation between two variables with no obvious direct link, name a plausible confounding variable that could be driving both.
description_for_ai: A spurious relationship is a correlation whose arithmetic is accurate but whose meaning is practically misleading, because there is no genuine direct connection between the two variables; it commonly appears when both variables are driven by the same unrecorded underlying factor. Before reporting any strong correlation, an analyst asks two questions: is there a believable, direct reason X would affect Y, and could a third, unmeasured factor explain both variables moving together. In a retail context, common hidden drivers include weather or temperature, seasonality, day of the week, and public holidays, since these can independently push multiple unrelated metrics up or down at the same time without either metric affecting the other.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Concluding a strong correlation justifies a specific business action (such as bundling two products together) without first checking for a plausible shared driver behind both variables. Failing to propose any specific alternative explanation when critiquing a spurious correlation claim, rather than naming a concrete candidate confounding variable. Assuming a correlation must be spurious just because it seems surprising, without actually checking whether a direct link is plausible first.
example_code_for_ai:
=CORREL(C5:C28,D5:D28)
' Returns 0.79 between two variables both plausibly driven by temperature, which was never recorded
' Neither variable causes the other; a third, unmeasured factor likely drives both

title: The Slope (SLOPE)
learning_objective: Calculate the slope of a regression line in Excel using SLOPE, and explain it as how much the outcome changes for each one-unit increase in the input.
description_for_ai: The slope of a regression line measures how much the dependent variable (the outcome being predicted) changes, on average, for every one-unit increase in the independent variable (the input used to predict it), calculated in Excel as =SLOPE(known_y_values,known_x_values), with the outcome range listed first and the input range listed second. A positive slope means the outcome rises as the input rises; a negative slope means the outcome falls as the input rises. The slope describes an average pattern across the whole dataset, not a guarantee for any single case.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Swapping the order of the two ranges, listing the input before the outcome, which SLOPE requires known_y (outcome) first and known_x (input) second. Treating the slope as a guarantee that applies to every single data point, rather than an average tendency across the dataset. Reading a small slope value as meaning 'no relationship' without also checking the units, since a slope's size depends entirely on the scale of the two variables being compared.
example_code_for_ai:
=SLOPE(D5:D28,C5:C28)
' D is Daily Sales (outcome), C is Marketing Spend (input)
' Returns 3.47: each extra currency unit of spend is associated with about 3.47 more in sales, on average

title: The Intercept (INTERCEPT)
learning_objective: Calculate the intercept of a regression line in Excel using INTERCEPT, and explain it as the model's predicted outcome when the input is zero.
description_for_ai: The intercept is the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable equals zero, calculated in Excel as =INTERCEPT(known_y_values,known_x_values), using the same outcome-first, input-second argument order as SLOPE. Together, slope and intercept build a complete prediction formula: outcome = intercept + (slope x input). The intercept should be treated as a mathematical starting point for the line, not necessarily a scenario that was ever actually observed in the dataset; some datasets produce an intercept that does not make literal real-world sense on its own, which does not automatically mean the model is wrong.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Reversing the known_y and known_x arguments, the same ordering mistake as with SLOPE. Interpreting the intercept as a real, observed data point rather than as the mathematical baseline the line happens to cross at zero input. Reporting the intercept on its own as a meaningful business figure without pairing it with the slope to form a usable prediction formula.
example_code_for_ai:
=INTERCEPT(D5:D28,C5:C28)
' Returns 171,491: the model's baseline sales estimate at zero marketing spend
' Combined with the slope, the full formula is Sales = 171,491 + (3.47 x Spend)

title: R-squared (RSQ) and What It Explains
learning_objective: Calculate R-squared in Excel using RSQ, and explain it as the share of variation in the outcome that the model actually accounts for.
description_for_ai: R-squared measures the proportion of variation in the dependent variable that is explained by the independent variable through the regression line, calculated in Excel as =RSQ(known_y_values,known_x_values) using the same outcome-first, input-second order as SLOPE and INTERCEPT, and always falls between 0 and 1. An R-squared of 0.61 means about 61% of the day-to-day differences in the outcome are explained by the input, with the remaining 39% coming from other factors the model does not capture. For a simple two-variable regression, R-squared is mathematically the correlation coefficient r squared, so a correlation of 0.78 corresponds to an R-squared of about 0.61.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Describing R-squared as 'the model is correct X% of the time,' which misstates what the statistic measures, it is the share of variation explained, not an accuracy rate. Treating a low R-squared as proof the analysis was done wrong, rather than as a genuine signal that the input alone does not explain much of the outcome. Forgetting the direct link between R-squared and the correlation coefficient from the prior topic, and recalculating from scratch rather than recognising R-squared equals r squared.
example_code_for_ai:
=RSQ(D5:D28,C5:C28)
' Returns 0.61 for the same marketing spend and sales data where CORREL previously returned 0.78
' 0.78 squared equals approximately 0.61, confirming the two statistics are directly linked

title: Making a Prediction with the Regression Formula
learning_objective: Combine an already-calculated slope and intercept into a single prediction formula, and use it to estimate an outcome for a specific input value.
description_for_ai: Once slope and intercept have been calculated separately, they combine into one prediction formula: outcome = intercept + (slope x input value), which can be built in Excel by referencing the slope and intercept cells directly rather than retyping their formulas, for example =(SlopeCell*InputValue)+InterceptCell. This lets an analyst answer a specific business question, such as what sales figure to expect for a stated spend amount, by substituting that one number into the formula rather than recalculating the whole regression again.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Retyping the full SLOPE and INTERCEPT formulas inside the prediction formula instead of referencing the already-calculated cells, making the workbook harder to audit and more error-prone. Reversing the order of operations, adding the intercept before multiplying the slope by the input value, rather than following outcome = intercept + (slope x input). Rounding the slope or intercept before using them in the prediction, which compounds small rounding errors into a noticeably wrong final estimate.
example_code_for_ai:
=(SlopeCell*40000)+InterceptCell
' With slope = 3.47 and intercept = 171,491, this returns approximately 310,463
' The prediction formula reuses the already-calculated slope and intercept cells rather than retyping them

title: Recognising Extrapolation Beyond the Tested Range
learning_objective: Given a regression model and a specific input value, determine whether that value falls inside or outside the range of data the model was built from, and explain why that matters.
description_for_ai: Extrapolation is using a regression model to predict an outcome for an input value that falls outside the range of values actually present in the dataset the model was built from. A model has no evidence for how the relationship behaves beyond the range it was tested on, so a prediction built on an extrapolated input is a guess presented with the appearance of a calculation, not a reliable estimate. The check is straightforward: compare the input value being predicted against the minimum and maximum of the independent variable's actual data range; if the input falls within that range, the prediction is reasonable; if it falls outside, the prediction should not be reported as reliable.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Reporting a prediction as reliable simply because the formula returned a number, without first checking whether the input value falls inside the tested range. Assuming a model that fits the tested data well must also hold true far beyond that range, when no evidence supports that assumption. Treating extrapolation as always wrong in every case, rather than specifically flagging it as unverified and requiring extra caution before it is acted on.

' Tested spend range: 8,584 to 69,535
Prediction at spend = 40,000   -> within range, reasonable estimate (~310,463)
Prediction at spend = 150,000  -> outside range, extrapolation, not reliable (~692,637)

title: When a High R-squared Still Hides a Poor Fit
learning_objective: Given a regression with a high R-squared and its scatter plot, identify whether the true relationship is actually curved rather than a straight line, and explain the consequence for the model's predictions.
description_for_ai: A high R-squared indicates a straight line accounts for most of the variation in the outcome overall, but it does not confirm that a straight line is the correct shape for the relationship at every point. Some real relationships rise steeply at first and then flatten out, a diminishing-returns curve, for example additional staff boosting sales quickly at low staffing levels but adding little once a shop floor or till capacity is reached. When the true relationship curves, a straight-line regression systematically over-predicts at both the low and high ends of the tested range even while overall R-squared looks strong, because the single straight line cannot bend to match the actual shape. The required check is always to build the scatter plot and visually compare the data's shape against a straight line before trusting R-squared alone.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating a high R-squared alone as sufficient proof that a straight-line model is trustworthy across the whole tested range, without ever building or checking the scatter plot. Assuming a curved relationship means regression cannot be used at all, rather than recognising the issue is that a straight line is the wrong shape for this particular relationship. Missing that a model can systematically over-predict at both extremes of a curved dataset even while its overall R-squared score looks impressive.
example_code_for_ai:
' R-squared = 0.85 for staff-on-shift vs daily sales, an apparently strong result
' Scatter plot shows sales rising steeply from 2 to 8 staff, then flattening
' Straight-line prediction at 2 staff (~276,893) and at 12 staff (~466,189) both over-predict the actual clustered data points

title: Stating the Null and Alternative Hypotheses
learning_objective: Given a business comparison between two groups, write a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis that correctly frame the question being tested.
description_for_ai: Every hypothesis test starts with two competing statements. The null hypothesis (H0) is the default assumption that there is no real difference between the two groups being compared, and that any observed difference is due to random variation; the alternative hypothesis (H1) is the statement that a real difference does exist. The null hypothesis is assumed true until the data provides strong enough evidence to move away from it, placing the burden of proof on demonstrating a difference rather than assuming one. For a before-and-after business comparison, H0 states the average outcome is the same in both periods, and H1 states the average outcome differs between the two periods.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing the alternative hypothesis as the default assumption instead of the null hypothesis, reversing which statement carries the burden of proof. Stating H0 and H1 in a way that overlaps or contradicts each other rather than being genuinely mutually exclusive. Skipping the hypotheses entirely and jumping straight to calculating a p-value, without first being explicit about what is actually being tested.
example_code_for_ai:
' No formula: this micro-topic is a written framing step before any calculation
H0: average daily sales are the same before and after the checkout lane pilot
H1: average daily sales are different before and after the checkout lane pilot

title: Calculating a p-value (T.TEST)
learning_objective: Calculate a p-value in Excel using T.TEST to compare two independent groups of data.
description_for_ai: A p-value answers a specific question: if the null hypothesis were true and there were really no difference, how likely is it that a difference this large would still appear purely by chance. It is calculated in Excel as =T.TEST(array1,array2,tails,type), where array1 and array2 are the two groups of raw values being compared, tails is set to 2 to detect a difference in either direction, and type is set to 3 for two-sample data where the two groups may have different amounts of spread, which is the safer default for real business data. T.TEST returns a single number between 0 and 1.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Mixing up which range is the before group and which is the after group, which does not change the p-value itself but can cause confusion when interpreting the direction of any difference found separately. Leaving tails or type at the wrong setting, for example using type 1 (paired) on two genuinely independent groups of days rather than type 3. Running T.TEST on ranges of unequal length that do not represent matched groups, producing a result that does not answer the intended question.
example_code_for_ai:
=T.TEST(B6:B25,E6:E25,2,3)
' B is 20 days of sales before a pilot, E is 20 days of sales after the same pilot
' Returns 0.0003 for one branch's pilot, and 0.80 for an identical pilot at a second branch

title: Interpreting a p-value Against the 0.05 Threshold
learning_objective: Given a calculated p-value, state whether the result is statistically significant using the 0.05 threshold, and phrase a non-significant result using precise language.
description_for_ai: 0.05 (5%) is a widely used, though not universally fixed, threshold for deciding whether a result counts as statistically significant: if p is less than 0.05, the result is unlikely to be random chance alone, described as statistically significant, leaning toward rejecting the null hypothesis; if p is 0.05 or higher, the result could plausibly be random chance, described as failing to reject the null hypothesis. Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not the same as proving the null hypothesis true, it means there is not enough evidence of a real difference, not that no difference exists. The precise phrase for a non-significant result is 'we do not have enough evidence that X changed,' never 'X was proven to have no effect.'
common_mistakes_for_ai: Describing a non-significant result as 'proof' that nothing changed, rather than as insufficient evidence of a change. Treating 0.05 as an absolute scientific law rather than a widely used convention that can vary by context or field. Reporting only whether a result is significant without also stating what that does and does not mean for the underlying business decision.
example_code_for_ai:
' No new formula: this micro-topic classifies an already-calculated p-value
p = 0.0003  -> below 0.05 -> statistically significant
p = 0.80    -> above 0.05 -> fail to reject H0, not 'proven no difference'

title: Statistical Significance vs Practical Importance
learning_objective: Given a statistically significant result and the actual size of the observed difference, judge whether the effect is large enough to justify a business decision, and explain why the two questions are separate.
description_for_ai: A statistically significant p-value indicates a difference is unlikely to be random noise, but it says nothing about whether that difference is large enough to matter for the business. With a large enough sample size, even a genuinely tiny, practically unimportant difference can become statistically significant, because larger samples make it easier to detect small effects, real ones and trivial ones alike. The required professional habit is to always report both the p-value and the actual size of the effect (in absolute terms and as a percentage of the baseline) together, and to weigh that effect size against the cost of acting on it, rather than treating a significant p-value alone as automatic justification for a decision.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating a statistically significant p-value as sufficient justification to approve a costly action without first checking how large the actual effect is. Assuming a large sample size makes a result less trustworthy, when it actually makes small, genuine effects easier to detect, which is exactly why effect size must be checked separately. Reporting a significant result without stating the effect size at all, leaving the reader unable to judge whether the finding is practically meaningful.
example_code_for_ai:
' 500 transactions before and after a new price display
Mean before = 2,484.09, mean after = 2,518.46, difference = 34.37 (about 1.4% of the average basket)
p = 0.026 (statistically significant), but the effect size alone does not justify a full rollout decision

title: Writing a Role-Context-Data-Constraints Prompt
learning_objective: Write a prompt asking an AI assistant to interpret a statistical result, including a role, business context, the verified data, and clear output constraints.
description_for_ai: A reliable prompt for statistical interpretation has four parts: a role (who the AI should act as, for example a data analyst assistant helping a branch manager), context (the business situation and what was actually tested), data (the real numbers already calculated and verified by the person prompting, never invented by the AI), and constraints (audience, length, tone, and what to avoid, such as 'do not claim causation unless the evidence supports it'). This mirrors the general prompting structure of context, data description, task, and output format, applied specifically to statistics. A vague prompt that only pastes numbers and asks 'explain this' invites a vague or overconfident answer; a specific prompt with explicit constraints gives the AI less room to overstate what the data shows.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Pasting raw numbers into a prompt with no role or context, producing a generic explanation disconnected from the actual business decision. Omitting constraints entirely, leaving the AI free to use confident causal language the data does not support. Letting the AI invent or estimate any data point instead of supplying every number already calculated and verified beforehand.
example_code_for_ai:
' Example prompt structure, not a formula:
'Role: you are a data analyst assistant helping a branch manager.
Context: we tested whether a checkout lane pilot changed daily sales.
Data: mean before = 283,100, mean after = 322,590, p-value = 0.0003.
Constraints: plain language, under 150 words, no unjustified causal claims.'

title: Catching Overstated Causation in an AI Response
learning_objective: Given an AI-generated statistical interpretation, identify any sentence that treats a correlation or regression result as proof of causation, and restate it accurately.
description_for_ai: AI assistants commonly turn a correlation or regression finding, which describes association, into language claiming direct causation, using phrases such as 'proves conclusively that X causes Y' or 'directly generating' an outcome. This overstates what the underlying statistics actually support: a regression or correlation result shows two variables move together, not that changing one variable is guaranteed to change the other, especially outside a controlled experiment. The correction keeps the useful finding but removes the unjustified causal claim, for example restating 'proves conclusively that spend causes higher sales' as 'spend and sales are strongly associated; this does not prove spend directly causes the increase.'
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting confident causal language in an AI response simply because the underlying numbers cited are accurate, when the numbers being correct does not make the causal claim correct. Failing to name the specific overstated phrase when flagging the error, giving a vague objection instead of quoting exactly what needs to change. Rewriting the causal claim as a weaker guess ('might possibly perhaps be related') rather than as a precise, still-useful statement of association.
example_code_for_ai:
' Flawed: 'proves conclusively that increasing marketing spend causes higher sales'
' Corrected: 'spend and sales are strongly associated; this does not prove spend directly causes the increase'

title: Catching a Misread p-value or R-squared
learning_objective: Given an AI-generated statistical interpretation, identify any sentence that misstates what a p-value or R-squared actually measures, and restate it accurately.
description_for_ai: Two specific misreadings recur often in AI-generated interpretations. First, describing R-squared as 'the model is correct X% of the time,' when R-squared actually measures the share of variation in the outcome explained by the model, not an accuracy rate. Second, describing a small p-value as 'only an X% chance the result had no effect' or as proof of near-certainty, when a p-value actually measures how likely the observed difference would be if the null hypothesis were true, not the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true. Both errors sound plausible and confident, which is exactly why they need to be checked against the precise definition each time rather than accepted at face value.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting a p-value or R-squared explanation because it sounds fluent and uses the right numeric value, without checking whether the definition attached to that number is actually correct. Correcting only one of the two misreadings when a response contains both, rather than checking every statistical term used. Restating the correction in language just as imprecise as the original, rather than tying it back to the exact definition taught for that statistic.
example_code_for_ai:
' Flawed: 'R-squared of 0.61 means the model is correct 61% of the time'
' Corrected: 'R-squared of 0.61 means about 61% of the variation in sales is explained by spend'
' Flawed: 'only a 0.03% chance the pilot had no effect'
' Corrected: 'if the pilot truly had no effect, a difference this large would only occur by chance about 0.03% of the time'

title: Catching an Unflagged Extrapolation
learning_objective: Given an AI-generated prediction and the range of data a model was tested on, identify whether the AI flagged an input value that falls outside that tested range.
description_for_ai: An AI assistant will readily compute a prediction for any input value handed to it, including one that falls far outside the range of data the underlying model was actually built from, and it will often present that prediction with the same confidence as one safely inside the tested range. Checking for this error requires comparing the input value used in the AI's prediction against the minimum and maximum of the actual tested data, a fact the AI response itself may never state. If the AI presents an out-of-range prediction without any caveat about the tested range, that omission is the error to flag, not the arithmetic, which is usually correct.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming a prediction is trustworthy because the AI stated it clearly and the arithmetic checks out, without independently checking whether the input value falls inside the tested range. Only checking the range when a number looks unusually large, missing cases where an out-of-range input produces a plausible-looking prediction. Flagging the entire response as unreliable rather than isolating the specific out-of-range prediction as the one problem needing a caveat.
example_code_for_ai:
' Tested spend range: 8,584 to 69,535
' AI states a prediction of 692,637 at 150,000 spend with no caveat
' Correct flag: 150,000 is far outside the tested range; this prediction should not be reported as reliable

title: Catching Confused Statistical vs Practical Significance
learning_objective: Given an AI-generated recommendation based on a significant p-value, determine whether the response also addressed the actual size of the effect before recommending action.
description_for_ai: An AI response can accurately report that a p-value is statistically significant while still giving flawed advice, by treating that significance alone as sufficient grounds for a costly recommendation, without ever stating or weighing the actual size of the effect. This error is often one of omission rather than an incorrect sentence: the response simply never mentions the effect size, or frames a large sample size as pure reassurance rather than as a reason the small effect was easy to detect. The correction requires both quantifying the effect size the response left out and adding a recommendation to compare that effect against the cost of acting on it, rather than treating the p-value as a green light on its own.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Focusing only on whether the p-value itself was reported accurately, missing that the flaw is the recommendation built on top of it. Failing to state the actual effect size in absolute or percentage terms when correcting the response, leaving the correction just as vague as the original. Concluding the recommendation must be entirely wrong, rather than recognising the statistical finding may be accurate while the leap to action is what is unjustified.
example_code_for_ai:
' AI response: 'p = 0.026, statistically significant, recommend immediate full rollout'
' Missing: the actual difference is only 34.37, about 1.4% of the average basket, from 500 transactions per group
' Correction: significance confirms the difference is likely real; it does not confirm a 1.4% lift justifies rollout cost

title: Applying the Full Five-Point Verification Checklist
learning_objective: Given a complete AI-generated statistical interpretation, run all five verification checks in sequence and produce a list of every issue found, including at least one omission.
description_for_ai: The full verification checklist for any AI-generated statistical interpretation has five points, applied in order: do the stated numbers match your own independently verified calculations; is any causal language ('proves,' 'causes,' 'guarantees') actually justified by the evidence; are the limits of the data respected, with no unflagged prediction beyond the tested range; is statistical significance kept separate from business importance, with effect size addressed; and is anything important missing entirely, not just misstated. Running all five points on a single response, rather than stopping after finding the first obvious error, is what distinguishes a genuine audit from a partial check, since a response can pass some checks while failing others.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Stopping the checklist after finding one clear error, rather than running all five points against the same response, since a single response frequently contains more than one distinct problem. Treating a response as fully verified because its stated numbers matched, without separately checking causal language, data limits, and significance versus importance. Skipping the fifth check for missing content, since it requires noticing what is absent rather than reading only what is present.
example_code_for_ai:
' A single AI response can fail multiple checklist points at once:
' 1) Numbers match -> yes  2) Causal language justified -> no  3) Data limits respected -> no
' 4) Significance vs importance kept separate -> not applicable here  5) Anything missing -> yes, no caveat on R-squared's meaning

title: Rewriting a Flawed AI Response into an Accurate Version
learning_objective: Given an AI response with identified errors, rewrite it into an accurate, business-ready version that keeps its accurate content and corrects only the flagged issues.
description_for_ai: Once every verification checklist issue in an AI response has been identified, the correction step rewrites only the flawed sentences, keeping the plain language, tone, and length constraints of the original response intact wherever they were already accurate. This is a targeted correction, not a rewrite from scratch: the goal is to preserve everything the AI got right (fluent plain-language phrasing, correct raw numbers) while fixing exactly the sentences flagged in the verification step, so the final version remains something a business audience can read easily. A rewritten response that discards accurate content along with the flawed content has not actually finished the task.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Discarding the entire AI draft and writing a completely new response from scratch, losing time and losing content that was already accurate and well-phrased. Correcting the flagged factual errors but leaving the confident, unjustified tone of the original unchanged elsewhere in the response. Introducing a new inaccuracy while rewriting, such as swapping an overstated causal claim for an equally unsupported claim in the opposite direction.
example_code_for_ai:
' Original (flawed): keeps accurate numbers, wraps them in unjustified causal language
' Corrected: same numbers, same plain language and length limit, causal language replaced with association language, extrapolation caveat added
